question.text: Rajiv has a ULIP policy purchased on 10th March 2024 with a sum assured of Rs.8,00,000. He pays an annual premium of Rs.3,00,000. At maturity, he receives Rs.42,00,000. What is the tax treatment of the maturity proceeds under Section 10(10D)?

answer.text: Fully exempt as ULIPs are covered under Section 10(10D) without any conditions
Exempt because the premium does not exceed 10% of sum assured
Not exempt under Section 10(10D) as the annual premium exceeds Rs.2,50,000 — proceeds taxable as capital gains
Exempt up to sum assured of Rs.8,00,000 and balance taxable as income from other sources

explanation.text: The Logic: For ULIPs issued on or after 1 February 2021, Section 10(10D) exemption is denied if the annual premium exceeds Rs.2,50,000. Rajiv's annual premium of Rs.3,00,000 breaches that high-premium threshold, so the maturity proceeds lose their Section 10(10D) exemption and the non-exempt ULIP is treated as a capital asset from FY 2025-26 onwards, with the gain taxable as capital gains. The policy also fails the 10-times-sum-assured framing applicable to life insurance policies generally (premium of Rs.3,00,000 is well above 10% of Rs.8,00,000), reinforcing the loss of exemption. The Trap: Option A ignores the Rs.2,50,000 ULIP-specific threshold. Option B mis-applies the premium-to-sum-assured ratio in Rajiv's favour — even on that test, Rs.3,00,000 is far above 10% of Rs.8,00,000. Option D invents a partial-exemption mechanism that is not part of Section 10(10D). Note: Both the 10-times-sum-assured framing (Section 10(10D) proviso) and the Rs.2,50,000 high-premium ULIP rule apply to ULIPs. Either failure independently disqualifies the policy from exemption.
